ch15.note: In Shakespeare's Hamlet, Fortinbras is the prince of Norway, not Sweden; the source's “Swedish prince” (瑞典王子) is an error, rendered here as printed. Contradicted by the play. It is a minor role, which is why the boy cast in it has leisure to read the whole tragedy.

ch15.anchor: the front door of St. Thérèse's Church
ch15.note: St. Thérèse's Church (小德肋撒堂), a real Gothic-style Catholic church with twin bell towers, dedicated to St. Thérèse of Lisieux (the “Little Flower”); 德肋撒 is the traditional Catholic transliteration of Thérèse/Teresa. Built on Datong Road (today Datian Road) in what is now the Jing'an district, its foundation laid on St. Thérèse's day, 3 October 1930, and opened a year later. Historical.

The International Funeral Parlor (万国殡仪馆), opened 1926 at the corner of Jiaozhou and Xinzha Roads, was the best-known funeral home of Republican Shanghai; the funerals of the film star Ruan Lingyu and the writer Lu Xun were held there. Historical.

“Wild pheasant” renders 野鸡 (literally “wild chicken”), old Shanghai slang for an unlicensed streetwalker who solicited on the streets rather than working from a registered house. The wife is accusing her husband of visiting prostitutes on his rounds, not of piety.
The Chinese dead were traditionally laid out on a door lifted from its hinges (门板), used as a plain bier before the body was coffined.

The “soft local speech” is the Wu topolect of the Shanghai region (吴侬软语, literally “the soft, tender speech of Wu”), famed for its gentleness; the priest, who first served in the north, reads instead in a Tianjin accent, a comic incongruity a local reader hears at once.
A funeral custom: a coin (口含钱, the “mouth-held cash”) was placed in the mouth of the dead, variously explained as fare for the journey below or to keep the mouth from gaping.

The undertaker's 门腔 is an obscure funerary term, evidently a made replacement for the missing tongue so the corpse may “speak”; the phrase is uncommon and the rendering “mouth-piece” is provisional. His point follows plainly: with the tongue gone, the dead man cannot cry out his wrong (喊冤) in the courts of the underworld.

“Opening a skylight” (开天窗), here said to be gang slang for a killing that leaves a hole in the back of the skull. The phrase is attested in other senses (burglary through a roof; the blank a censor left in a newspaper), but its use as an execution method is not corroborated in the reference sources; given as the neighbors' talk.

“Planting a lotus” (种荷花) is attested Shanghai underworld argot for disposing of a victim in the Huangpu River. Paired here with “opening a skylight” as the gangs' private punishments (家法, “house law”). Corroborated at the level of popular gang-history writing.

ch16.note: In the seven-week mourning sequence a rite is held every seventh day; the seventh of these, on the forty-ninth day (7×7), is the “last seventh” (断七, literally “breaking the seven”), after which formal mourning ends. Corroborated.

ch16.anchor: the slave of a conquered country
ch16.note: “Slave of a conquered country” renders 亡国奴, a bitter wartime epithet for a people living under foreign conquest, one of the era's most charged words. The postman's refusal to become one is offered as the reason he died.

An Eight Immortals table (八仙桌) is a square hardwood table seating eight, named for the Eight Immortals of Daoist legend; it stood at the center of a household's main room, for meals, guests, and, as here, a boy's calligraphy practice.

Hongkou (虹口), the district north of Suzhou Creek, was the heart of Shanghai's Japanese settlement (“Little Tokyo”) and of its military and intelligence organs; the “special-service station” (特务机关) was such an organ. Historical.

ch17.anchor: A letter from home is worth ten thousand in gold
ch17.note: The postmaster quotes a famous line of Du Fu (杜甫), from “Spring View” (春望), written in 757 amid the An Lushan rebellion: 烽火连三月，家书抵万金 — “The beacon-fires have burned three months on end; a letter from home is worth ten thousand in gold.” Corroborated.

Huang Tingjian (黄庭坚, 1045–1105) was a leading Song poet and one of the great masters of calligraphy; to have copied his running-hand models marks the letter-writer as a cultivated man, not the ordinary correspondent a postman sees. Historical.

The Siming Apartments (四明公寓, part of the Siming Village lane compound) were built in 1932 as staff housing for the Siming Bank, in the French Concession on Rue Ratard (巨籁达路, named for a French consul; renamed Julu Road in 1966). Historical.

Yu Hongjun (俞鸿钧, 1898–1960; known in English as O.K. Yui) was mayor of Shanghai at the time of the 1937 Japanese invasion (formally from late July to mid-November 1937). Historical. The source prints his name 俞鸿均; the attested figure is 俞鸿钧, and the name is corrected here.
The clock tower of the Maritime Customs House on the Bund, whose Westminster-chiming clock (“Big Ching”) was completed in 1927, was one of the waterfront's chief landmarks. Historical.

The London plane trees that line the old French Concession streets are called 法国梧桐 (“French parasol-trees”) in Chinese; their leaf-canopy is a signature of that quarter of Shanghai and recurs through the story.

The 88th Division (八十八师) was a German-trained elite infantry division of the National Revolutionary Army, one of the units Chiang Kai-shek rushed to the 1937 Battle of Shanghai, where it took catastrophic losses. Historical.
Chen Sunong (陈素农, 1900–1983), a Whampoa Academy graduate, is recorded as major-general chief of staff of the 88th Division. A real officer; corroborated.

ch17.anchor: See a snake and you'll strike it rich
ch17.note: A folk belief: the snake, a “little dragon,” is read as an omen of a coming windfall (见蛇必发, “see a snake and you're sure to prosper”) — hence the lottery ticket. Corroborated as a common belief, though not a universal one; some regions read a snake as ill luck.

ch18.note: The Special Naval Landing Forces (海军陆战队), Japan's marine infantry, were garrisoned at Hongkou; their action opened the Battle of Shanghai on 13 August 1937. Historical. (The battle itself is noted earlier, at The Rebel, installment 3.)

Jintan are small aromatic medicinal pellets taken as a breath-freshener and pick-me-up. The source's 人丹 is the Chinese domestic brand, launched to answer the Japanese original 仁丹 (also “Jintan”), the two the subject of a Sino-Japanese trademark war. Material culture; corroborated.
They are playing Chinese chess (象棋). The chariot (車), which moves and captures in straight lines to any distance, is the game's most powerful piece, answering to the rook.

ch19.note: “Fourth Avenue” is Sima Road (四马路, literally “fourth horse road”), today Fuzhou Road; in the Republican era it was Shanghai's street of brothels, teahouses, and publishing houses at once. Historical.

ch19.anchor: the political commissar of the Songjiang detachment
ch19.note: A political commissar (政委) is the Communist Party's political officer within a military unit, ranking beside its commander; the Songjiang detachment was a Party-led guerrilla force in the countryside southwest of Shanghai.

The Kempeitai (宪兵), the Imperial Japanese Army's military police, were notorious in occupied China for torture and summary execution; they are distinct from the Tokkō, the special higher (political) police noted earlier in The Rebel. Historical.

The Shanghai Municipal Police of the International Settlement recruited Sikhs from the Punjab from 1884; their turbans (often described as red), beards, and height made them a fixture of the streets, and they drew the mocking nickname 红头阿三 (“red-turban number three”). Historical.

From the late 1930s Shanghai took in tens of thousands of Jewish refugees fleeing Nazi Europe, being one of the few ports that required no visa; many settled in Hongkou. The stranger now in Su Lina's old flat is a quiet marker of that displacement. Historical.

ch19.anchor: sauced duck from Lu Gao Jian
ch19.note: Lu Gao Jian (陆稿荐) is a celebrated cooked-meats house of Suzhou origin, a “time-honored brand,” best known for its sauced pork and sauced (braised) duck (酱鸭). Material culture; corroborated.

ch20.note: A catty (斤) is the Chinese pound, in the Republican era standardized at about 500 grams (600 grams historically); half a catty is thus roughly half a pound of tea.
“Cement” renders 水门汀, the Shanghainese phonetic borrowing of the English word “cement,” a relic of the treaty-port pidgin; by extension it means a concrete pavement. Corroborated.

Biluochun (碧螺春, “green snail spring”) is a famous green tea from the Dongting hills by Lake Tai near Suzhou, ranked among China's finest; the measure is the tael (两), about 37 grams. Material culture; corroborated.

ch20.anchor: broken at the Battle of Changsha
ch20.note: The Battles of Changsha (长沙会战) were fought between 1939 and 1944. Historically the 88th Division's near-annihilation, and the famous remnant of “eight hundred,” belong not to Changsha but to the 1937 defense of Shanghai — the “Eight Hundred Heroes” (八百壮士) of the 88th's regiment at the Sihang Warehouse. The novel appears to transpose that episode onto Changsha; it is rendered here as the source has it, with the discrepancy noted.

The “Queen of the Dance World” (舞林皇后) was the title given the reigning dance-hostess, often decided by a paying ballot; the wartime “benefit dances” (募捐义舞) turned such contests to raising relief funds for the resistance.

ch20.anchor: when Wang Jingwei became Foreign Minister in 1935
ch20.note: Corroborated: Wang Jingwei held the Foreign Minister's portfolio, concurrently with the premiership, until he was shot and resigned in November 1935. (Wang Jingwei is noted more fully at The Rebel, installment 1.)

A concubine (姨太太) was a formally kept secondary wife; the polygynous household of the wealthy persisted well into the Republic despite the new Civil Code. Su Lina's refusal is a refusal of that place.
